..The upper pattern this morning is defined by an 
amplified trough of low pressure along the West Coast with a low
center observed early this morning near the Bay Area of 
California, Hurricane Polo (a category 3 hurricane with maximum 
sustained winds of 120 mph near 23.2N/114.0W or west of the tip 
of the Baja, moving N at 10 kts), and a subtropical ridge across
the majority of Mexico.

The latest satellite and radar imagery indicated a band of clouds/
mainly light showers with a few embedded thunderstorms that extend
from what was left of post tropical cyclone Odalys (near 23N/123W)
into west central Arizona, with storms beginning to expand east
across central Arizona. These storms coincide with a thin axis of
deformation aloft at 500 mb between the trough and the subtropical
ridge in Mexico. The latest GOES precipitable water imagery indicated
deep tropical moisture with PWATs 2.00+ inches along the entire Gulf
of California this morning, assisted by the strong SLY flow up
the Gulf along the easterly envelope of Hurricane Polo. Across
SE AZ this morning, PWATs generally range from 1.10-1.25 inches
from Tucson southeast and 1.25-1.50 inches west of Tucson. 

Expect showers and thunderstorms to expand in coverage today
(especially this afternoon) as the deep tropical moisture moves
northeast into SE AZ and the general deformation/lift aloft 
expands across the area. With PWATs generally above 1.50 inches 
across the entire CWA, this is an anomalously moist airmass (3.0
to 3.5 standard deviations above the norm). Precipitation
amounts will generally be light through this afternoon, with 
rainfall amounts between a tenth and quarter inch (higher 
amounts near a half inch south and east of Tucson and the higher
terrain).

Showers and thunderstorms really start becoming widespread with
moderate-to-locally heavy rainfall tonight as the upper-low
amplifies and moves SE to the Colorado River along the AZ/CA 
state line by 29/12Z Tuesday morning. That thin axis of 
deformation aloft at 500 mb shifts east overnight, positioning 
itself from south-central Pima county to Tucson to Safford by 
daybreak. This is where things get interesting. We begin to see 
strong moisture flux convergence in the lower-levels (850-700mb)
into the same area of this deformation/lift aloft. This should 
not only feed the deeper moisture into an enhanced area of storm
development, but it will allow for storms to train Tuesday 
morning with newer development favored to the SW toward the 
deeper moisture. This is supported by the 28/00Z HREF 3-hr QPF 
PMM neighborhood probabilities in this area, with probabilities 
between 70-90% for 1.00+ inch and 10+% 3.00+ inches between 
29/12-18Z Tuesday. This may make the morning commute across the 
Tucson Metro Area and farther NE in Safford a bit messy Tuesday 
morning if very heavy rainfall amounts are focused along this 
axis. This can also be complicated as we move into the afternoon
Tuesday, as the front itself moves from west to east across 
Southeast Arizona resulting in another focus for heavy rainfall.

The heaviest rain will occur Monday night into Tuesday afternoon
with expected rainfall amounts during this time period between
0.75-1.25 inches with as much as 2-3" inches possible in those 
areas impacted by training of storms (repeated rounds of pcpn) 
and upslope regions in the higher terrain (especially the 
Catalina/Rincon/Pinaleno Mountains). Rainfall runoff will result
in running water in normally dry washes and roadway dips with 
significant ponding of water likely in low-lying areas and other
flood-prone locations. Isolated to scattered locations may 
experience flash flooding with this event. Longer-term heavy 
flows will also be possible into Tuesday night into Wednesday 
within main-stem drainages due to widespread heavy rainfall. 
There is a Flash Flood Watch in effect from 11 AM MST today 
through 11 PM MST Tuesday evening. 

One side-note, severe storms will be possible Tuesday...but
should be considered a secondary threat compared to the risk of 
flash flooding. As the upper-level low tracks across the area,
decent forcing, marginal CAPE and abundant shear will be
present. Therefore, expect strong to perhaps isolated severe 
storms...with brief transient low-top supercells also possible.

Otherwise, lingering instability and moisture will be present 
Wednesday for additional shower activity, but drier air will 
quickly lower precipitation chances through the day. A ridge of
high pressure then builds into the Desert Southwest the second 
half of the work week, shutting down thunderstorm activity.
